questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to cook tasty meals with fewer ingredients
Why food is becoming cheaper in the UK
How farmers grow vegetables in glasshouses
Food shortages and the future food supply
questions.why: They discuss recent food shortages and ask how much longer a stable, affordable supply will continue.

questions.q: What caused the recent shortages of eggs, tomatoes and cucumbers in the UK?
options: Cold weather and rising energy prices
A long strike by farmers and drivers
A very hot and dry summer in Europe
New rules on imports from abroad
questions.why: Rob says the problems were caused by unusually cold weather combined with rising energy prices.

questions.q: Why are some UK farmers selling their apple orchards?
options: Because apples are no longer popular
Because of climate change
Because production costs are rising
Because the government asked them to
questions.why: They sell to housing developers rather than struggle with increasing production costs.

questions.q: Why does Adam Leyland find the forecast 'extraordinary'?
options: Because production is rising so fast
Output is falling despite big investment
Because records began only a few years ago
Because food prices will fall sharply
questions.why: He notes the huge investment in glasshouses and polytunnels, yet production is forecast to be the lowest on record.

questions.q: What does Professor Charles Godfrey mean by 'de-globalising'?
options: Countries are less connected and buy food nearer
Countries are importing more food than ever
People are eating less food to save money
Farmers are moving abroad to find cheaper land
questions.why: He says we live in a less connected world, and deglobalisation means sourcing food nearer home.

questions.q: What worries Professor Godfrey about deglobalisation?
options: It will make food taste worse than before
It will cost farmers too much to change
It will stop people eating local food
It may be harder to feed places short of food
questions.why: He worries it makes it harder to supply food to parts of the world that can't produce enough.

questions.q: How much does Professor Godfrey think global demand for food will rise in 30 to 40 years?
options: By 10 to 20 percent
By 30 to 50 percent
It will double
It will stay the same
questions.why: He says global demand will probably rise 30 to 50 percent.

questions.q: What is Professor Godfrey's own view about UK land use?
options: The UK should stop farming and focus on nature
The UK should only grow food for itself
Smart planning can boost food and nature
The UK should import almost all of its food
questions.why: He says if we plan land use in a canny way, we can produce more food and increase biodiversity.
